## Web Searcher: Navigation & gesture law — both platforms, including back-gesture conflicts

Research question: "Native mobile interface design conventions that a DESIGNER must decide, for iOS and Android, current as of 2026. Narrow scope — platform design law only, not implementation code. Cover exactly these: (1) Apple's current design language and Human Interface Guidelines direction as of 2025-2026, including the Liquid Glass material introduced at WWDC 2025 for iOS 26 — what it actually is, where it applies, what it demands of a designer, and what Apple says NOT to do with it; (2) Google's Material 3 and Material 3 Expressive — current status, what Expressive changed, and its stated research basis; (3) navigation models and when each is correct: iOS tab bar vs Android bottom navigation bar, navigation stack and back behavior including Android's system back and predictive back, sheets and modals, iOS NavigationSplitView vs Android navigation rail; (4) the numeric specifications a designer must hit: minimum touch target sizes (Apple 44pt vs Material 48dp — verify both from primary sources), default type scales and body text sizes, spacing and margin baselines, and corner radius conventions; (5) safe areas and system regions — status bar, home indicator, Dynamic Island, display cutouts, edge-to-edge and the Android 15+ mandatory edge-to-edge change; (6) gesture systems and their conflicts — iOS interactive pop gesture and Android back-swipe versus author-built horizontal swipe affordances such as carousels and swipe-to-delete; (7) what genuinely differs between the two platforms such that a single design cannot serve both, and where a cross-platform neutral design is legitimate. Prioritize primary sources only: developer.apple.com Human Interface Guidelines, m3.material.io, developer.android.com. Reject blog restatements where a primary source exists."

Your angle: **Navigation & gesture law — both platforms, including back-gesture conflicts** — Pillars 3 and 6 together, since the back gesture is a navigation mechanism: when a tab bar vs bottom nav vs nav rail vs split view is correct, sheet/modal rules, Android system back and predictive back semantics, and the documented collision between edge-swipe navigation and author-built horizontal swipe (carousels, swipe-to-delete) plus the sanctioned mitigations.
Search query: `iOS tab bar vs Android navigation bar navigation rail NavigationSplitView predictive back gesture interactive pop gesture swipe conflict carousel developer.android.com developer.apple.com design guidance`

## Task
Use WebSearch with the query above (or a refined version). Return the top 4-6 most relevant results.
Rank by relevance to the ORIGINAL question, not just the search query. Skip obvious SEO spam/content farms.
Include a short snippet capturing why each result is relevant.

Structured output only.

{"hookSpecificOutput":{"hookEventName":"SubagentStart","additionalContext":"PONYTAIL MODE ACTIVE — level: full

# Ponytail

You are a lazy senior developer. Lazy means efficient, not careless. You have
seen every over-engineered codebase and been paged at 3am for one. The best
code is the code never written.

## Persistence

ACTIVE EVERY RESPONSE. No drift back to over-building. Still active if
unsure. Off only: "stop ponytail" / "normal mode". Default: **full**.
Switch: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.

## The ladder

Stop at the first rung that holds:

1. **Does this need to exist at all?** Speculative need = skip it, say so in one line. (YAGNI)
2. **Already in this codebase?** A helper, util, type, or pattern that already lives here → reuse it. Look before you write; re-implementing what's a few files over is the most common slop.
3. **Stdlib does it?** Use it.
4. **Native platform feature covers it?** `<input type="date">` over a picker lib, CSS over JS, DB constraint over app code.
5. **Already-installed dependency solves it?** Use it. Never add a new one for what a few lines can do.
6. **Can it be one line?** One line.
7. **Only then:** the minimum code that works.

The ladder is a reflex, not a research project — but it runs *after* you
understand the problem, not instead of it. Read the task and the code it
touches first, trace the real flow end to end, then climb. Two rungs work →
take the higher one and move on. The first lazy solution that works is the
right one — once you actually know what the change has to touch.

**Bug fix = root cause, not symptom.** A report names a symptom. Before you
edit, grep every caller of the function you're about to touch. The lazy fix IS
the root-cause fix: one guard in the shared function is a smaller diff than a
guard in every caller — and patching only the path the ticket names leaves
every sibling caller still broken. Fix it once, where all callers route through.

## Rules

- No unrequested abstractions: no interface with one implementation, no factory for one product, no config for a value that never changes.
- No boilerplate, no scaffolding "for later", later can scaffold for itself.
- Deletion over addition. Boring over clever, clever is what someone decodes at 3am.
- Fewest files possible. Shortest working diff wins — but only once you understand the problem. The smallest change in the wrong place isn't lazy, it's a second bug.
- Complex request? Ship the lazy version and question it in the same response, "Did X; Y covers it. Need full X? Say so." Never stall on an answer you can default.
- Two stdlib options, same size? Take the one that's correct on edge cases. Lazy means writing less code, not picking the flimsier algorithm.
- Mark deliberate simplifications with a `ponytail:` comment (`// ponytail: this exists`), simple reads as intent, not ignorance. Shortcut with a known ceiling (global lock, O(n²) scan, naive heuristic)? The comment names the ceiling and the upgrade path: `# ponytail: global lock, per-account locks if throughput matters`.

## Output

Code first. Then at most three short lines: what was skipped, when to add it.
No essays, no feature tours, no design notes. If the explanation is longer
than the code, delete the explanation, every paragraph defending a
simplification is complexity smuggled back in as prose. Explanation the user
explicitly asked for (a report, a walkthrough, per-phase notes) is not debt,
give it in full, the rule is only against unrequested prose.

Pattern: `[code] → skipped: [X], add when [Y].`

## Intensity

| Level | What change |
|-------|------------|
| **full** | The ladder enforced. Stdlib and native first. Shortest diff, shortest explanation. Default. |

Example: "Add a cache for these API responses."
- full: "`@lru_cache(maxsize=1000)` on the fetch function. Skipped custom cache class, add when lru_cache measurably falls short."

## When NOT to be lazy

Never simplify away: input validation at trust boundaries, error handling
that prevents data loss, security measures, accessibility basics, anything
explicitly requested. User insists on the full version → build it, no
re-arguing.

Never lazy about understanding the problem. The ladder shortens the
solution, never the reading. Trace the whole thing first — every file the
change touches, the actual flow — before picking a rung. Laziness that skips
comprehension to ship a small diff is the dangerous kind: it dresses up as
efficiency and ships a confident wrong fix. Read fully, then be lazy.

Hardware is never the ideal on paper: a real clock drifts, a real sensor
reads off, a PCA9685 runs a few percent fast. Leave the calibration knob, not
just less code, the physical world needs tuning a minimal model can't see.

Lazy code without its check is unfinished. Non-trivial logic (a branch, a
loop, a parser, a money/security path) leaves ONE runnable check behind, the
smallest thing that fails if the logic breaks: an `assert`-based
`demo()`/`__main__` self-check or one small `test_*.py`. No frameworks, no
fixtures, no per-function suites unless asked. Trivial one-liners need no
test, YAGNI applies to tests too.

## Boundaries

Ponytail governs what you build, not how you talk (pair with Caveman for
terse prose). "stop ponytail" / "normal mode": revert. Level persists until
changed or session end.

The shortest path to done is the right path.
"}}

## Predictive Back Gesture Design Guidance (developer.android.com)

Predictive back navigation respects gesture insets defined in edge-to-edge features, and you should avoid adding touch gestures or drag targets under these gesture areas.

For full-screen surface animations, when a user performs a back gesture on a full-screen surface, the inner area should scale down as the gesture progresses, and as soon as the user crosses the commit threshold, the contents should swap to the next state using a fade through.

Feed the progress value with a STANDARD_DECELERATE token or PathInterpolator so the gesture is more apparent in the beginning, which enhances movement detection at the start of the gesture and employs deceleration.

## Edge-to-Edge Considerations

System gesture insets apply to gesture-navigational areas used by the OS that take priority over your app. This is particularly important when implementing predictive back gestures, as you need to respect these reserved areas.

## Navigation Rail vs. Bottom Navigation Bar (Material 3)

**Window Size Context:**
- Compact windows (smaller than 600dp, such as a phone in portrait orientation) should always use a navigation bar.
- The collapsed nav rail can be used in medium Window widths from 600dp to 839dp, such as a tablet or foldable in portrait orientation.

**Ergonomic Advantages:**
The navigation rail is more ergonomic and visually balanced due to hand placement on larger devices and large spacing between nav items.

**Key Constraint:**
Never use the navigation rail and navigation bar simultaneously.

The search results show that navigation rail is preferred for medium and larger screen sizes (600dp+), while bottom navigation bars are designed for compact phone displays.

Based on the search results from developer.android.com, here's what I found about system gesture exclusion rects, gesture navigation conflicts, and app swipe handling:

## System Gesture Exclusion Rects

To maintain functionality of elements on the left and right edges of the screen, you can opt out of the back gesture selectively by indicating to the system which regions need to receive touch input using the View.setSystemGestureExclusionRects() API introduced in Android 10. This method is also available in ViewCompat as of androidx.core:core:1.1.0-dev01.

## Gesture Navigation Conflicts

The gesture navigation model might conflict with gestures that were previously used by app developers, and you might need to make adjustments to your app's user interface as a result. The new system gesture for back is an inward swipe from either the left or the right edge of the screen, which might interfere with app navigation elements in those areas.

## Edge-to-Edge Design

If your app uses gestures or has controls in the system gesture areas, it may create conflict with system-wide gestures, and the goal is to use insets to avoid gesture conflicts. Additionally, you can use the Gesture Exclusion API for controls, such as drag handles, that need to reside in the gesture zones.

## Carousel and Horizontal Swipes

Avoid horizontal carousels when designing for Wear OS. When seekbars or similar controls are too close to the bottom gesture area, users can accidentally trigger the home gesture when they complete a horizontal swipe.

results.title: Ensure compatibility with gesture navigation | Android Developers
results.snippet: The single most load-bearing primary source for the back-gesture-vs-author-swipe collision. States that Android's system back is an inward swipe from EITHER the left or right edge, that this 'might conflict with gestures that were previously used by app developers,' and names the two sanctioned mitigations: (1) go edge-to-edge and use system gesture insets (getSystemGestureInsets / mandatorySystemGestureInsets) to keep controls out of the reserved zones, and (2) View.setSystemGestureExclusionRects() (Android 10+, also in ViewCompat 1.1.0+) to selectively opt regions out of the back gesture — explicitly scoped to controls like drag handles and sliders, with a documented per-edge exclusion height cap so it cannot be abused to disable back wholesale. This is the page that tells a designer that a full-width carousel or swipe-to-delete row sitting under the edge zone is a real, documented defect and what the platform-approved fix is.

results.title: Predictive back design | Mobile | Android Developers
results.snippet: Apple has no equivalent of this, which is exactly why it matters for the 'what genuinely differs' pillar. Google's designer-facing (not code) spec for predictive back: the semantics of the peek/commit threshold, that the inner surface scales down as the gesture progresses and content swaps via fade-through once committed, and motion tokens (STANDARD_DECELERATE / PathInterpolator) so movement reads at the start of the drag. Critically it repeats the conflict rule from the design side: predictive back respects the gesture insets defined by edge-to-edge, and designers should 'avoid adding touch gestures or drag targets under these gesture areas.' Establishes that on Android, back is a previewable, cancellable, animated navigation state — a designed transition the designer owns, not a free system behavior.

results.title: Tab bars | Apple Developer Documentation
results.snippet: Primary source for the iOS side of the top-level navigation decision, and current for iOS 26 — the tab bar is now a floating Liquid Glass element that can shrink/hide on scroll and, on iPad, adapt into or coexist with a sidebar. Key designer law here: tab bars are for peer top-level sections only, tab selection must persist per-tab navigation state, tabs must never be used to perform actions, and you should avoid hiding or disabling tabs. This is the article that contrasts with Material's navigation bar and is the anchor for the 'iOS tab bar ≠ Android bottom nav' distinction (Apple caps practical tabs low and pushes overflow to a More tab; Material caps at 5 and forbids overflow).

results.title: Navigation rail – Material Design 3
results.snippet: Gives the numeric window-size law that decides bottom navigation bar vs navigation rail — the Android counterpart to iOS NavigationSplitView/sidebar adaptation. Compact windows (<600dp, phone portrait) must use the navigation bar; the collapsed rail is valid from 600dp–839dp (tablet/foldable portrait); the rail is called out as more ergonomic and visually balanced at larger sizes given hand placement. Hard constraint stated outright: never use the navigation rail and navigation bar simultaneously. This is a breakpoint-driven rule with no iOS equivalent — Apple switches on size class and idiom, Material switches on dp window-size class — and is a genuine 'one design cannot serve both' case.

results.title: Sheets | Apple Developer Documentation
results.snippet: The iOS modal-presentation law. Covers when a sheet is correct (a scoped task closely related to the current context, retaining context of the parent) versus a full-screen modal or a pushed screen, plus detents/resizable heights, the drag-to-dismiss gesture and why a sheet that holds unsaved work must confirm before dismissing, and the iOS 26 Liquid Glass treatment where sheets pick up a glass edge and inherit the background's tint. Directly relevant to gesture conflict: a sheet's vertical drag-to-dismiss competes with scrollable content inside it, the same class of collision as horizontal edge-swipe vs carousel. Pair with the HIG's Modality article for the 'when is modality justified at all' rule.

results.title: Gestures | Apple Developer Documentation
results.snippet: Apple's primary statement of iOS gesture law and the iOS half of the conflict analysis: standard system gestures (edge swipe back / interactive pop, swipe-up home indicator, Control/Notification Center pulls, Dynamic Island interactions) are reserved, and custom gestures must not redefine or interfere with them. Establishes that the interactive pop gesture is a user expectation the designer inherits — disabling it to make room for an author-built horizontal swipe is a regression, and the sanctioned pattern is to keep full-width horizontal swipe affordances (carousels, swipe-to-delete rows) out of the leading screen edge or make them inset. Note the page is JS-rendered, so it must be read in a browser rather than fetched as static text.
